questions.q: What is the key difference between a login and a user in SQL Server?
options: A login is a server-level principal that authenticates to the instance; a user is a database-level principal a login maps to
A login and a user are simply two names for the exact same object
A user authenticates to the instance; a login is scoped to one database
Logins are only used for Windows authentication, users only for SQL authentication
questions.explain: Logins operate at the server/instance level; users are the database-scoped principals that logins map to, and that permissions are granted to.

questions.q: Where does sys.server_principals live, and what does it list?
options: It's a server-level view (queried from any database) listing every login and server role on the instance
It exists only inside msdb and lists Agent job owners
It's database-scoped and lists only that database's users
It only exists on Azure SQL Database, not on-premises SQL Server
questions.explain: sys.server_principals is instance-wide, listing logins and server-level roles regardless of which database you're connected to.

questions.q: How are sys.database_principals rows linked back to sys.server_principals rows?
options: By matching the sid column between the two
By matching the name column exactly, case-sensitively
There is no reliable link — you must ask the login owner directly
By matching the create_date column
questions.explain: A database user's sid should match the sid of the server login it maps to; a mismatch or missing login indicates an orphaned user.

questions.q: What does membership in the fixed server role sysadmin grant?
options: Full control of the entire SQL Server instance
SELECT permission on every table in one specific database
The ability to only view backup history in msdb
Read-only access to sys.server_principals
questions.explain: sysadmin is the highest fixed server role, granting unrestricted control over the whole instance.

questions.q: What does the fixed database role db_datawriter grant?
options: INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE on every table in that database
Full ownership control of the database
The ability to create new logins on the server
SELECT-only access to every table in that database
questions.explain: db_datawriter grants write access (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) across every table in the database it's assigned in; db_datareader is the SELECT-only counterpart.
